t: Cells with Odd Values in a Matrix — Editorial
o:
We start with an all-zero m x n grid. Each operation [r, c] adds 1 to every cell in row r and every cell in column c, so a cell (i, j) ends up with value (number of operations touching row i) + (number of operations touching column j). We must count cells whose final value is odd.

**Example 1:** m=2, n=3, indices=[[0,1],[1,1]]. Row counts: row0 gets 1 op, row1 gets 1 op → [1,1]. Column counts: col0 gets 0 ops, col1 gets 2 ops, col2 gets 0 ops → [0,2,0]. Cell (i,j) = rowCount[i] + colCount[j]: matrix = [[1,3,1],[1,3,1]] — all 6 cells are odd → answer 6.

**Example 2:** indices=[[1,1],[0,0]]. Row counts [1,1], column counts [1,1]. Every cell = 1+1 = 2 (even) → answer 0.

Constraints are tiny (m, n ≤ 50, ≤100 operations), so even a full simulation is fine; but the counting insight gives the O(m + n + k) follow-up solution.
k: A cell's final value depends only on how many times its row was incremented plus how many times its column was incremented.
A cell is odd exactly when its row count and column count have different parities.
Answer = (#odd rows)*(#even cols) + (#even rows)*(#odd cols), computable without touching the matrix.

a.i: Keep the actual matrix and literally perform each operation: increment all cells of row r and all cells of column c. Finally scan the matrix and count odd values. This mirrors the problem statement directly and works easily within constraints.
s: Initialize an m x n matrix of zeros.
For each [r, c] in indices, add 1 to every cell in row r and every cell in column c.
Scan all cells and count those with odd values.
a.t: O(k * (m + n) + m * n) where k = indices.length — each operation touches a whole row and column, then one final scan.

a.i: We never need the matrix. Track only how many times each row and column is incremented. Cell (i, j) has final value rowCount[i] + colCount[j], which is odd iff the two counts differ in parity. So if there are R odd rows and C odd columns, the answer is R*(n - C) + (m - R)*C. This achieves the O(m + n + k) time / O(m + n) space follow-up.
s: Build rowCount[m] and colCount[n] arrays by tallying each index pair.
Count R = number of rows with odd rowCount, C = number of columns with odd colCount.
Odd cells come from (odd row, even col) pairs and (even row, odd col) pairs.
a.t: O(k + m + n) — one pass over indices to tally, one pass over each count array.
a.sp: O(m + n) for the two count arrays.

w: In an interview, mention simulation first to show you understand the problem, then immediately present the parity-counting approach as the optimal solution — it directly answers the follow-up. Common pitfalls: forgetting that a cell at (r, c) gets incremented twice per matching index (once from the row, once from the column); miscounting when deriving the formula (odd cell ⇔ row and column parities differ). Edge cases: repeated identical indices (counts just accumulate), a single row or column, and all-even results like Example 2. Possible follow-ups: what if increments could be negative or large (only parity matters, so use XOR/parity throughout), or if you had to output the actual matrix (then use a difference-array trick to build it in O(k + m*n)).
